newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico goes for growth in optimistic plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico goes for growth in optimistic plan.

text.p: A far-reaching programme setting out Mexico's goals for growth to the next millennium brought words of caution from analysts who said key targets looked optimistic.

Outlining its economic plans to the turn of the century in its National Program for Financing Development, the government said it was aiming for five percent growth on average each year, and targetting inflation of 7.5 percent and a current account deficit of 3.2 percent of GDP by the year 2000.
Analysts agreed fulfilling the whole plan would be a challenge, but Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner denied it was overly optimistic.

"The goals were realistic, and I think that the president has defined very well an ambitious and realistic programme," he told reporters after Ernesto Zedillo presented it at his official Los Pinos residence.
"It is ambitious because (the economy) will start to grow in a sustainable manner and bring the country back to (the growth levels) we had in the 1970s," he said.
But economists questioned how attainable the goals actually were, particularly the target for 5.6 percent GDP growth projected for the 2000 presidential election year.

"GDP growth higher than 5.0 percent is a very ambitious goal -- I think they can get it in 1998 and 1999 but it's not so sure for the year 2000," said Sergio Martin, chief economist for Mexico at ING Barings here.
Ann Ginsberg at Valores Finamex said the GDP and the inflation forecasts looked challenging.

"Growth and inflation in the year 2000 look optimistic," she said, but added that the current account projection of 3.2 percent of GDP looked more credible than the 2.0 percent set out in a previous plan in 1995.
"By easing up on the current account side they are lending more credibility to the plan," she added.

Another analyst feared the size of the projected current account deficit could weigh on growth. "The current account deficit projection is still fairly small and that would limit growth rates, which makes them look optimistic," he said.

Some economists also questioned how the government could confidently posit such targets just a month before mid-term congressional elections, in which the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party looks destined to loose its majority.
"There is a question mark over how the new Congress will affect (the plan)," Ginsberg said.
One economist said the up-beat programme was aimed at winning votes just before the July 6 polls.
"The numbers are good but the government knows reality is not as good as the numbers, they know people are discontented," he added.
ING Baring's Martin said the forecast rise in domestic savings to 18 percent of GDP would not be easy to attain.
"My impression is that public savings will not be strong in the next two to three years," he said. "Even though it's possible, it's not going to be as rapid as they say."

He cited extraordinary spending to sustain the banking sector as a consequence of the 1994-95 peso crisis, programmes to help debtors and costs involved in continuing to finance public sector pensions.
But making the pieces of the economic jigsaw fit required the factoring in of a weaker peso, Martin said.
"Assuming a current account deficit this low and inflation moving down slowly implies a weaker peso," he said. "If the peso gets weaker these goals get some credibility."
But he said it was time to start discussing growth rather than just stabilising the economy. "After the house was burned down they had to think about rebuilding it," he said.
